### Question 1

A reservoir is where a germ lives full time: its address, not its exit door and not its ride. There are three kinds of addresses: people (an infected wound, bacteria carried in someone's nose), animals (a bat, a rodent, a farm animal), and the environment (soil, standing water in a humidifier reservoir). The test is whether the organism can actually grow and reproduce there. A bed rail that got contaminated an hour ago usually fails that test, so it is a surface a germ was dropped onto, not a home. The distinction changes your action: you treat or remove a reservoir, but you clean a surface.

### Question 2

Each step in the chain only happens if the previous one did. A germ that never leaves its reservoir cannot ride anywhere; one that rides but finds no way in cannot infect. So you do not have to defeat the organism at every step, you only need one step to fail. That is why a unit can attack whichever link it controls best: cleaning shared equipment and hand hygiene attack the ride, tissues and masks attack the exit, vaccination attacks susceptibility. Any one of those, done reliably, ends that particular transmission.

### Question 3

Trace the journey in order: the organism exists (agent), it lives somewhere (reservoir), it gets out (portal of exit), it travels (mode of transmission), it gets in (portal of entry), and it meets someone whose defenses cannot stop it (susceptible host). Two quick checks catch nearly every wrong version: exit must come before entry, because you cannot arrive somewhere you have not left for, and the new host must come last, because that is where the trip ends. Any list that violates either rule is describing spread in reverse.

### Question 4

One question separates the two: did anything carry the germ in between? If a person hands it to a person, by touch or by a cough landing on someone at close range, that is direct. If a doorknob, a shared cup, a droplet nucleus drifting across a room, or a mosquito did the carrying, that is indirect. Notice what the split is not about. It is not about which organism, not about hospital versus community, and it does not let the receiving person off the hook. Either route still ends at someone whose defenses can be breached.

### Question 5

The portal of exit is the doorway an organism uses to get out of the body it is currently in, and for respiratory viruses that doorway is the nose and mouth. A tissue cures nothing: the virus is still multiplying in the airway, so the reservoir is untouched, and the person's immunity is unchanged. What the tissue does is catch secretions at the instant they leave. Blocking exit is efficient because one action protects everyone downstream at the same time, which is why source control is a first move in respiratory outbreaks.

### Question 6

Arriving is not the same as invading. The definition of a portal of entry requires access to tissue where the organism can multiply, and unbroken skin does not provide that. No cut, no mucous membrane contact, no line or catheter tunneling under the barrier, and the chain simply ends there. One caution keeps this from being falsely reassuring: organisms sitting on intact skin are not harmless, because hands carry them onward to eyes, noses, and wounds, which are real entry points. The barrier holds only as long as the germ stays where it landed.

### Question 7

Vectors and vehicles are both middlemen for germs, and the sorting rule is simply alive or not alive. Water, food, a shared cuff, a bed rail: inanimate, so vehicle. A mosquito, tick, or flea is alive and seeks out hosts on its own, so vector. Some vectors are only couriers carrying the organism on their bodies, while in others the organism actually develops inside the insect before it can be transmitted. The reason the split matters is that the countermeasures share nothing: you can disinfect a vehicle, but you cannot disinfect a mosquito.

### Question 8

Equipment that moves between people is one of the most reliable rides a germ ever gets, and rides belong to the mode-of-transmission link. Check what disinfecting actually changes: the first client is still colonized or infected, so the reservoir is intact; that client's exit routes are unchanged; and the next client still has a fingertip that will be punctured, so the entry point is unchanged. The only thing you eliminated was the vehicle. Glucose meters are the classic example because they touch blood and travel from room to room.

### Question 9

Nearly all infection prevention works by keeping the organism away from the person. Vaccination is the exception: it allows the encounter to happen and changes the result. By presenting the immune system with a harmless preview, it builds antibodies and memory cells in advance, so an arriving pathogen is much more likely to be neutralized quickly, and illness that happens anyway is usually milder. Seasonal flu vaccine lowers the odds rather than removing them, which is why vaccinated staff still perform hand hygiene and stay home when ill. Shifting those odds is exactly what the susceptible-host link means, because susceptibility is a property of the person rather than of the germ's route. Anything that raises host defenses, such as vaccines, correcting malnutrition, or controlling blood glucose, belongs to this link.

### Question 10

Colonized and infected are different states. Infected means the organism is causing tissue damage and symptoms; colonized means it is simply living and reproducing on or in the body without causing trouble. Since a reservoir is defined by where an organism lives and multiplies, a colonized person is a reservoir, regardless of how well she feels. Her nostrils are the exit door of that reservoir, not the reservoir itself, and calling a person a vehicle is wrong because vehicles are inanimate. This is why routine practices do not depend on already knowing who is infected.

### Question 11

When a unit is saturated with a pathogen, ask which measure removes the supply and which ones only intercept it in transit. Hand hygiene and equipment disinfection intercept, and both are worth doing, but virus keeps being produced as long as someone on the unit is shedding it. A person with active vomiting and diarrhea is producing enormous quantities of norovirus, so removing that person from the setting removes the reservoir itself. The 48-hour rule after symptoms stop exists because shedding outlasts symptoms, which is why feeling better is not the criterion for returning.

### Question 12

A urinary catheter is two things at once: a road and a residence. It is a road because organisms can travel up the outside of the tube along the urethra, or up the inside from a contaminated drainage bag, reaching a bladder that the urethra and normal voiding usually protect. It is a residence because within days the plastic becomes coated in biofilm, a slime layer where organisms grow while shielded from antibiotics and immune cells. You cannot scrub biofilm out of a tube that is inside someone, so the intervention that actually works is time: fewer catheter days, and no catheter placed without a real indication.
